html:
The first practical windmills in the world, built in Sistan, on today's border of Iran and Afghanistan, by the 7th to 9th centuries. They ground grain and lifted water.

Unlike later European mills, they turned on an upright shaft. Sails of reed matting or cloth were fixed around the shaft, and tall mud-brick walls shielded one side, so the wind pushed the sails round like a revolving door. Sistan suits them: a strong wind blows steadily from the north for about 120 days each summer. Arab geographers of the 9th and 10th centuries describe the region's mills, and a tradition says the man who murdered the caliph Umar in 644 was a Persian skilled in building them.

Like the qanat, they show how farmers of dry Iran made the most of scarce resources, here wind instead of water. Windmills appeared in Europe in the late 12th century, but with the shaft lying flat and sails facing the wind, which gave more power. Whether the idea travelled from Iran, perhaps through the Islamic world or the Crusades, or arose on its own is unclear.
